- The first page loads when the tab opens: **Settings ▸ Grid ▸ Rows per page** rows (1,000 at first), in the table's
  key order, so pages follow one another. A table with an AUTO_INCREMENT key opens newest first, until you sort it
  (**Settings ▸ Grid ▸ Open tables newest first**).
- The status bar says how many rows are loaded and of how many: `1,000 of about 52,000 rows`. The total is the server's
  estimate until you click **Count Exactly** (**Data ▸ Pages ▸ Count Rows Exactly**), which runs `COUNT(*)` with the filter.
  An estimate below what has already loaded is left out (InnoDB's can say 0 of a million rows), and with no figure to go
  by, Load All and an unindexed sort ask first. After the count comes the time the rows were read: `· read 14:32`.
- **Load More** (⌥⌘↓) loads the next page; **Load All** (⌥⇧⌘↓) loads every row that's left, in batches as they arrive.
  Above **Settings ▸ Grid ▸ Load All asks above** rows (100,000 at first) it asks first: every row is held in memory
  while the tab is open. Cancel it in the status bar's activity: what arrived stays, and Load More and Load All carry
  on from there.
- Anything slow here (a page, a filter, a sort, Load All, Count Exactly, Column Summary) can be stopped with **⌘.**, the
  toolbar's Cancel or the status bar's activity. A cancelled page leaves the rows as they were; Refresh (⌘R) loads them.
- Pages are read by offset. If someone adds or deletes rows between pages, a row can repeat or be missing: a notice says
  so when it happens, and Refresh reads the rows again.
- **↓** or **Page Down** on the last row loaded loads the next page too.
- The pager at the right of the toolbar shows which rows are on show and steps through them: **First Page**, **Previous
  Page**, **Next Page** and **Last Page** (which counts the rows first) replace the rows, where Load More adds to them.
  **Rows per Page** changes the page size for this tab.
- A long value (TEXT, BLOB, JSON, a very long VARCHAR) comes cut at the server, to its first 1,000 characters
  (**Settings ▸ Grid ▸ Long values**; 0 reads every value whole), so a table of large blobs opens at once. Such a cell ends
  in `…`. **Data ▸ Load Full Cell**, or the button in the value panel, reads the rest. Editing the cell, copying it,
  Duplicate Row and exporting read the whole value first, so nothing written or copied is ever the cut text; a quick filter
  on a cut cell asks for Load Full Cell first. Search on the loaded rows and Find look only at what's loaded.
  A table with no key can't find a row to read it back, so its values come whole.
- A hidden column isn't read at all. Showing it again loads the rows again.
- **View ▸ Refresh** (⌘R) reads the table's columns and loads the rows shown again; **View ▸ Refresh Every** does it by itself every 5 to 60 seconds or a number you type (**Custom…**),
  until you choose **Off**. Pending changes stay.

**Data ▸ Sort ▸ Order By…** takes any ORDER BY, expressions included; a click on a header's sort control replaces it. On a
read-only connection it's checked like a typed filter.

**Data ▸ Copy Table's Query** copies the SELECT the tab runs, with its filter and sort, and **Open Table's Query in a Tab** opens it in
a new query tab.

## Filter, search and sort

**Filter** and **Search** hide the rows that don't match; **Find** (⌘F) leaves every row and moves between matches.
**Find Text on Server** looks through every table, not only this one.

The chip at the left of the grid bar always says where filtering runs: **On server** (every row of the table, loaded or
not) or **Local** (only the rows loaded so far, at once, with no query).

- **Filter**: type a condition, as you would after WHERE, for example `status = 'paid' AND total > 100`, and press Return. A leading `WHERE` is
  fine. It is coloured as SQL, as in the query tab, and the field grows as the condition wraps, up to eight lines (then
  it scrolls); ⌥↩ starts a new line. Suggestions show as you type: columns, then operators,
  then the column's values (read from its first 10,000 rows), then AND and OR. ↑ and ↓ choose, Tab inserts, ⎋ closes, and
  ⌥⎋ brings them up anywhere. The clock (or ⌥↓ in the field) lists the table's last
  20 filters; the ⓧ, or **Data ▸ Clear Filter**, shows every row again. The filter and the sort are kept for the next
  time the table opens. On a read-only connection, the whole SELECT must pass the
  [read-only check](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/read-only-queries.html): a condition that calls a function such as `SLEEP` or `GET_LOCK` isn't sent,
  and the bar under it says why. The **?** at the bar's end opens [Read the data in a grid](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/data-grid.html).
- **Search all columns** (⇧⌘E) finds rows with the text in any column, as HeidiSQL does: text and JSON columns with
  `LIKE`, numbers and dates as text, binary columns by a whole `0x…` value. Tick **Loaded rows only** to search just the
  loaded rows instead.
- Search and `LIKE` read the text a cell shows, BIT digits and JSON included. Whether they ignore case is the column's
  collation: `utf8mb4_bin` and other binary ones don't, and JSON follows the connection's.
- **Quick Filter**: right-click a cell for `=`, `<>`, `<`, `>`, `LIKE` (starts with, ends with, contains), `IS NULL` and
  `IS NOT NULL` with its value, and `IN` / `NOT IN` with every value selected in its column. Each item shows its SQL.
  Hold ⌥ to add the condition to the current filter with `AND`. The clipboard's text is offered too. **Data ▸ Quick
  Filter** has the same conditions by name (Less Than Selection, Contains Selection, In Selected Values…); ⌃⌘1 and ⌃⌘2
  filter by the focused cell's value, equal and not equal.
- **Type a Value…** (in both Quick Filter menus) asks for the value: choose how to compare (`=`, `<>`, `<`, `>`, starts
  with, contains, ends with), type the value, and press **Filter**. Tick **Add to the current filter** to keep the
  filter there is and add the condition with `AND`.
- **Filter by Values…** (the funnel on a column's header, shown on hover and on a filtered column; **Data ▸ Filter by
  Values…**; or a header's menu): the column's values with how many rows have each, counted on the server within the
  current filter (the 1,000 most frequent). Tick the ones to show, or type part of a value and press **Contains**. The
  funnel opens over the rows and replaces its own earlier choice, so you can widen it again. In
  **Column Summary…**, a click on one of a column's most frequent values adds it to the filter.
- **Sort**: double-click a header, or click the arrow at its right, to sort by that column, ascending, then descending,
  then not at all. To sort by several columns, ⇧-click the next column's arrow (⌥ works too, and ⌥-double-click on a
  header), or right-click its header for **Add to Sort**; each arrow shows its place in the order. **Data ▸ Sort ▸ Sort by
  Columns…** (or a header's menu) sets several at once: a line per
  column, each **Ascending** or **Descending**; the arrows move a column up or down the order, **Add Column** adds one
  and the minus takes it away. Rows sort on the server, and rows the sort leaves equal go in key order, so pages never
  repeat or miss a row (a view or a table without a key has no such order). On a table of over a million rows, sorting
  by a column without an index asks first (**Settings ▸ Safety**, on at first). With **Loaded rows only** ticked, the
  loaded rows sort here instead, as plain text without case or accents, or by value in number columns: the server's
  collation can order them otherwise, and an ENUM goes by its text.
- **Find** (⌘F) and **Find and Replace** (⌥⌘F) work on the loaded rows: ⌘G and ⇧⌘G go to the next and previous match,
  the bar says `3 of 12`, and every match is tinted, as are the cells Search All Columns found. **Options** has Match
  Case, Regular Expression (`$1` in the replacement), Whole Words and Filter Rows, which hides the loaded rows without a
  match. Replacements are pending edits, like any other. A long value is read whole first, so what comes back is all of it.

## Edit rows

Nothing is written until you apply. Leaving a row writes nothing.

- **Edit a cell**: type over it, double-click it, or press Return or F2 (as in HeidiSQL). ⌫ starts with the cell empty.
  Return keeps the edit, Esc cancels, Tab moves to the next cell. Select several cells and type: each gets the value its column takes. Record View and Transpose edit
  the same way.
- **Values are checked as you keep them**, by the column's type and the server's sql_mode, as Apply will write them: a
  number too big for its column, a third decimal in `DECIMAL(10,2)`, a day the month doesn't have, a word that isn't
  one of an ENUM's. The editor then stays open and says why under the cell: fix the value or press Esc. Typing is never
  blocked, and numbers and DECIMAL travel as the text you typed, so nothing is rounded on the way.
- **Each type has its editor**:
  - BOOLEAN, TINYINT(1) and BIT(1) show a checkbox. Space, Return or a double click ticks or clears it; typing `t`,
    `f` or `n` sets true, false or NULL.
  - An ENUM shows its values in a list over the cell; a SET a checklist, where **Set** keeps the ticked ones. Typing
    still works: `read,write`.
  - Dates and times are typed as `YYYY-MM-DD hh:mm:ss`, with fractional seconds when the column keeps them; ↑ and ↓
    step the part under the cursor (the day, the hour…). Zero dates are kept where sql_mode allows them, TIMESTAMP
    values are in the session's time zone, and a NULL cell starts empty: it never fills in today's date.
  - Bytes (BINARY, BLOB, shapes) are typed as hex: `0x00FF`. BIT shows and takes every bit: `b'1010'` or `1010`.
  - A value of more than 256 characters, or of several lines, opens in the value panel (below).
  - A foreign key shows the rows of the table it refers to, each as "label (key)", the label being that table's
    first text column, or the one you chose with **Use as Label** (below). They are searched on the server as you
    type, by label or by key, 100 at a time, so a big table is never listed whole. Return or a double click puts the
    key in the cell. **Data ▸ Foreign Keys ▸ Choose Referenced Row…** opens the same list.
- **The value panel** (⇧↩) edits the selected cell too: ⌘↩ or clicking elsewhere keeps the text as a pending edit,
  Esc puts the cell's value back. A value the column refuses stays there, and the panel says why. Its **⋯** menu has
  **Format JSON** and **Compact JSON**, **Load from File…** (a file's bytes in a binary column, else its UTF-8 text)
  and **Save to File…**.
- **Data ▸ Set Value ▸ Insert Value** (and a cell's right-click menu) puts in a value the server works out when Apply runs:
  `NULL`, `DEFAULT`, `NOW()`, `UTC_TIMESTAMP()`, `CURDATE()`, `CURTIME()`, `UNIX_TIMESTAMP()`, `UUID()`, `UUID_SHORT()`
  or a random value, whichever fit the column. Until then the cell shows it in grey: `ƒ NOW()`.
- **Data ▸ Add Row** (⌘I) adds a new row after the loaded ones. Where the server fills a value in, the new row says so
  in grey: *auto* (AUTO_INCREMENT), *default*, *generated*. **Duplicate Row** (⌘D) copies the selected rows, and
  their AUTO_INCREMENT columns show *auto* for the server to number; **Duplicate Row Without Keys** (⇧⌘D) leaves every
  key column to the server too.
  **Delete Rows** (⌘⌫, or ⌫ on rows selected by their numbers) marks the selected rows for deletion. **Cut** (⌘X) copies
  the selected cells and clears them: NULL where the column allows it, else empty. **Set Expression…** (⌃⇧F2) sets them to any SQL expression or function, sent as you typed it when you apply. **Set NULL** (⌥⌘N) and **Set DEFAULT** set the selected
  cells.
- **Edit ▸ Paste** (⌘V) puts cells copied from Excel, Numbers or a grid (tab-separated, or CSV) into the cells from the
  selected one on, as pending edits: numbers with a comma for decimals and dates such as `31.12.2026` or `12/31/2026`
  are read the way the column's values are written. Rows past the last loaded one become new rows, and one value pasted
  over several selected cells fills them all. Cells that can't go in their column are listed first, so you can paste
  the others or nothing. **Data ▸ Paste as New Rows** adds every copied row as a new one. A cell reading `NULL` (the
  grid's NULL text) is NULL.
- When the copied cells could be read two ways, the **Paste Format** sheet asks first, starting from AirSQL's guess:
  what separates the cells (lines of commas or semicolons without tabs may be CSV), the decimal mark (numbers such as
  `1,234`), and the order of day, month and year (dates such as `03/04/2026`). **Data ▸ Paste with Format…** always
  asks.
- **Data ▸ Foreign Keys ▸ Related Rows** (⌃⌘↓) lists the row a foreign key cell points to and the rows of other tables that point to
  the selected row; choosing one opens that table filtered to them.

### Foreign key labels and virtual foreign keys

- A one-column foreign key's cell shows the row it refers to in grey after its value (before it, for a number): the
  referenced table's label, read from the server for the rows on screen only. Right-click a column header of the
  referenced table and choose **Use as Label** (also in the Data menu) to show that column instead of its first text
  column; choose it again to go back.
- Many schemas have no real foreign keys. Right-click a column header and choose **Add Virtual Foreign Key…** to say
  which table's key the column holds (AirSQL guesses from the name: `customer_id` → `customers`). AirSQL keeps it on
  this Mac with the table's view settings, never in the database. The drop-down, Related Rows (both ways), the labels
  and the [ER diagram](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/editors.html#the-er-diagram) then follow it as a real foreign key. **Remove Virtual Foreign Key**
  forgets it.
- Pending changes have their colours: an edited cell amber, a new row green, a row to delete struck through in red.
  The bar under the grid bar counts them.
- **Undo** (⌘Z) and **Redo** (⇧⌘Z) step through the pending changes (a paste or a multi-cell edit is one step);
  **Revert** (⌥⌘Z) discards the selected rows' changes, **Revert All** every one.
- Pending changes are kept on disk as you make them. If AirSQL quits or the Mac restarts, they come back the next time
  you open the table, marked "Kept from before".
- Closing the tab with pending changes asks whether to keep them for later or throw them away. Quitting AirSQL lists,
  in one sheet, the tables with pending changes and any transaction still open in a query tab (which is rolled back).

### Which tables can be edited

AirSQL addresses each row by its primary key, or, without one, by the first unique key whose columns can't be NULL. Key
values are never shortened, so a change always reaches exactly its row. A table with neither is read-only, and the bar
says why; so are views. Generated columns can't be edited.

## Apply changes

- A table a single click shows, in the preview tab, keeps its pending changes when you click another table: the tab
  stays open with its dot, and the next table gets a preview of its own.
- **Data ▸ Apply Changes** (⌘S) writes every pending change in one transaction on the data session: deletes first (in
  batches of 500), then edits, then new rows. Each edit's `UPDATE` names the row by its key and the edited cells by the
  values you loaded (`` `price` <=> 10 ``), and each statement must change exactly its rows. If one changes another
  number (someone else changed a cell you edited, or deleted the row, since it was loaded) or the server refuses one,
  everything is rolled back, nothing is applied, and the grid selects the row; when the server's error names a column
  ("Data too long for column 'note'", "Column 'name' cannot be null", a duplicate value of a unique key), it selects
  that cell. Fix the value and apply again; if someone else got there first, revert the change, reload the rows and
  make it again. Changes kept over a restart are checked the same way.
- **Manual Commit** (the toolbar's transaction pop-up, or Query ▸ Transaction Mode) moves the table tab to a session of its
  own. Each Apply then writes into a transaction left open, and the rows you read show those changes, until **Commit** or
  **Roll Back**. Each Apply is still all or nothing. Closing the tab or quitting with the transaction open asks first. If the connection
  drops, the tab says the server rolled the transaction back, with how many rows, and nothing is applied until you press
  **Open New Session**; the rows are then read again. A deadlock ends the whole transaction too: Apply says so, and the
  rows are read again.
- What Apply can't check: FLOAT, TIMESTAMP, JSON, spatial and vector values, dates with a zero month or day and values
  over 64 KB don't compare exactly, so edits to those go by the key alone and overwrite what is there; the preview
  names them. A change that only differs in case or trailing spaces can pass on a column whose collation ignores
  those. Rows to delete go by their key: someone else's change to a row doesn't stop its delete, and neither does a
  change to a column you didn't edit stop your edit.
- **Preview SQL…** shows the statements first, in the [SQL preview](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/sql-preview.html). The preview also comes first on
  connections where **Settings ▸ Safety ▸ Show the SQL before the grid's Apply** is on (every Production connection),
  and whenever there is a warning: a table on MyISAM, Aria, MEMORY or another engine that can't roll back, or deletes
  that also change other tables through `ON DELETE CASCADE` or `SET NULL`.
- Values are checked again as Apply writes them; one that no longer fits (sql_mode changed, or it came from a find
  and replace) stops Apply before anything runs, and the grid selects its cell.
- After Apply, new rows stay where they were and show what the server filled in, their AUTO_INCREMENT key (the insert
  ID) and defaults included: each is read back by its key. When every row of the table (or of the filter) is loaded,
  the edited rows are read back by their keys and the deleted ones go, so nothing else loads again; otherwise the
  loaded rows load again. A new row's untouched cell shows **auto**, **default** or **generated**, in the value panel
  too, until Apply.

## Copy and export

These work in a query's results too.

- **Edit ▸ Copy** (⌘C) copies the selected cells in the format last chosen in **Copy As** (TSV at first); in a query tab
  result with nothing selected, every row. **Copy with Headers** (⌥⌘C) puts the column names first. Values are copied
  whole, as stored, whatever **Display As** shows. **View ▸ Grid ▸ View As ▸ Text** shows the rows in the same format.
- **Edit ▸ Copy As** ▸ TSV, CSV, Pipe-Separated, JSON, JSON Lines, Markdown, HTML Table, XML, Pretty Table, One Row, SQL INSERT, INSERT with many rows, INSERT IGNORE, REPLACE,
  UPDATE, DELETE, WHERE Clause or IN List (the selected values, quoted and split by commas, to go in `IN (…)`; NULLs are
  left out). The SQL formats address rows by the key, and UPDATE and DELETE add any of it you
  didn't copy; without a key, by every column copied. The one you choose becomes ⌘C's format.
- The export sheet previews the first rows in the format chosen; CSV can use a comma, semicolon, tab or pipe.
- **Data ▸ Export Rows…** (and a result tab's **Export Result…**) saves the selected rows, the loaded rows (with their
  pending changes) or every row of the table with its filter and sort, streamed from the server on a session of its own, as CSV, TSV, JSON, JSON Lines, SQL,
  Markdown, HTML, XML or an Excel workbook (.xlsx). Choose whether the column names come first, how NULL is written
  (`NULL`, `\N` or nothing), CSV's separator (any text) and quotes, Windows line endings, the file's encoding (UTF-8, with
  or without a BOM, UTF-16, Windows-1252 and others; characters it lacks are replaced, and you're told), whether line breaks
  inside values become spaces and whether the file opens afterwards, then **Export…** to a file or **Copy** to the clipboard.
  In a workbook, exact numbers over 15 digits (a 20-digit id, a long DECIMAL) go as text, as Excel would round them,
  and a value over Excel's 32,767 characters a cell is cut: AirSQL says how many were, and CSV keeps them whole.
  Hidden columns aren't exported, and the sheet says how many are left out. SQL formats leave out generated columns.
  In CSV a real NULL has no quotes and the text NULL has them, so Import tells them apart; TSV has no way to.
  CSV is UTF-8 without a BOM, which scripts read as it is: Excel for Mac needs **Data ▸ From Text**.
  XML and HTML can't hold control characters, nor can a workbook: each shows as �.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/data-grid.html

# Read the data in a grid

A table's rows and a query's results show in the same grid. These parts of it help you read what is there: the
status bar's figures, the value panel, Record View, Transpose, other ways to show a column, colours, text, charts, and
a column's summary. Loading, filtering, editing, copying and exporting a table's rows are on
[A table's rows](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/table-data.html).

## The toolbar

A table tab and a console result each have a row of buttons over the rows: the actions that are also in the menu bar, kept
beside the work. The buttons act on the grid under them, wherever the focus is. Hold the pointer over one to see what it
does, or why it's dimmed. A table's has the Data, Structure, DDL switch, Refresh, Refresh Every, Add Row, Duplicate Row, Delete Rows and Apply; Revert
and Preview SQL are on the bar that shows with pending changes. Every grid has Find, the Column List, Sort by Columns, the Value Panel, Record View, Transpose, View As and
Chart. A console result adds Pin, Compare With and Export, and shows its editing buttons only when it can be edited. When
the tab is narrow, what doesn't fit moves to the **»** menu at the end of the row, the same at that width however you got there;
Add Row, Delete Rows, Apply, Find and Sort stay longest.

## The header

Each column's header shows its name and, under it, its type. Marks before the name tell you about keys:

- a gold key: the primary key, or the unique key the grid uses to find a row when there is no primary key;
- a 1 in a circle: another unique key; an outline key: an index;
- a chain link: a foreign key.

After the type, **auto** marks an auto-increment column, **generated** a generated one, **default** a column with a
default value, and **null** a column that allows NULL. Hold the pointer over a header for all of this in words and the
column's comment.

## The status bar

With cells selected, the status bar shows the focused cell (**r3 : c5**, row and column), how many cells are
selected, and one figure for them: their sum, or their count when they aren't numbers. Click the figure to see them
all (count, sum, average, smallest, largest, median, distinct values) and choose the one shown. Sums of decimals are
exact; a whole column's figure says **of loaded rows** while the table has more. Only whole numbers add up: dates,
version numbers, phone numbers and BIT values get a count. **Edit ▸ Copy Selection Summary** (⇧⌘C) copies every figure.
Selections of more than 100,000 cells aren't added up. In a narrow window the figure, then the focused cell, make way for the rest; a table's row count and its **Count
Exactly**, **Load More** and **Load All** stay. Right-click them to copy what they say, or to count or load rows.

## Move around

- **Data ▸ Go to Row…** (⌘L) goes to a row by its number, or to `column:row`, the column by its name or number:
  `email:120`.
- **View ▸ Grid ▸ Column List…** (⌘J) lists every column. Type to find one; Return (or a double-click) jumps to it; its box,
  or Space, shows or hides it; **Show All** brings back hidden columns.
- **Edit ▸ Extend Selection** (⌥↑) grows the selection from the focused cell to its column, then its row, then
  everything; **Shrink Selection** (⌥↓) goes back the same way.
- Hold ⇧ to scroll a mouse wheel across, and ⌥ to scroll five times as far.
- **Data ▸ Columns ▸ Hide Column** hides the selected columns. A column comes back where it was.
- **Data ▸ Columns ▸ Freeze** keeps the columns up to the focused one (the key column, say) at the left while you scroll across.
  Choose it on the last frozen column to unfreeze them. AirSQL remembers it for each table.
- Esc closes the find bar, leaves Record View and Transpose, then narrows the selection to the focused cell.
- Drag a header to move its column, drag its right edge to resize it, and double-click the edge to fit its values.
  AirSQL remembers the columns' order, widths, hidden and frozen columns and display types for each table, and for
  each query in the query tab, so they open as you left them.
- **View ▸ Text Size ▸ Bigger** (⌘+) and **Smaller** (⌘−) change the grid's text size while it has the focus; **Actual Size** (⌘0)
  goes back to the size in Settings ▸ Grid.

## See a whole value

- **View ▸ Value Panel** (⇧↩) opens the focused cell's whole value beside the grid, never shortened: as wrapped text,
  as a JSON tree, as hex, or as a picture when the bytes are an image. It follows the cell you select. A double-click
  on a cell you can't edit opens it too.
- **View ▸ Grid ▸ Record View** (⌥⌘R) shows the focused row as a form, a line per column. **Previous** and **Next** above it
  (or **View ▸ Grid ▸ Previous Record** ⌥⌘← and **Next Record** ⌥⌘→) move between rows; **Back to the Grid** returns. A double-click
  on a row's number opens it. In a table, its values can be edited there as in the grid. A filter or a sort on a
  query result shows the grid again, as does an Apply that deletes the row.
- **View ▸ Grid ▸ Transpose** (⌥⌘T, the grid's right-click menu, or the toolbar) turns rows
  into columns, with the column names down the left: handy for comparing a few wide rows. A query result with one row opens this way; **Settings ▸ Grid ▸ Transpose results with one row** turns
  that off. Transpose shows the first 1,000 rows.

## Show a column another way

**Data ▸ Columns ▸ Display As** (also on a cell's right-click menu) changes how the selected columns look, not what they hold:
copying and editing use the stored value.

- Numbers: **Number with Grouping**; **Decimal Places ▸** rounds them (half up) to none, 1, 2, 3 or 4 decimal places,
  grouped by thousands as your Mac groups them; or **Date from Unix Time** (seconds or milliseconds), in your time zone.
- Dates: **Short**, **Medium** or **Long Date and Time**, as your Mac writes dates (System Settings ▸ General ▸ Language
  & Region). A DATE column shows the date only. Zero dates, TIME and YEAR stay as stored.
- A TIMESTAMP cell's tooltip names the session's time zone, which the value is shown in.
- **Time Zone ▸** (DATETIME and TIMESTAMP columns) moves the values: **From UTC to This Mac's** takes them as UTC and
  shows them in your time zone; **From This Mac's to UTC** does the reverse. A TIMESTAMP arrives in the session's time
  zone, so choose the first one when that is UTC. The header says so (`datetime as medium date, UTC → this Mac's`).
- Bytes: **UUID** (for `binary(16)`), **Hex**, or **Text (UTF-8)**.
- **As Stored** shows the value as the server sent it again. AirSQL remembers each column's choice for each table.

**Detect from the Bytes** shows a 16-byte value as a UUID and readable bytes as text, and leaves the rest as stored. **UUID,
Time First** reads a value stored with MySQL's `UUID_TO_BIN(x, 1)`.

A spatial column can show as **Well-Known Text** (`POINT(1 2)`). Dates can also use **Settings' Date Format**, a pattern
you set in **Settings ▸ Grid ▸ Date format**, such as `dd/MM/yyyy HH:mm`.

## Other commands on cells and columns

- **Data ▸ Columns ▸ Hide Other Columns** keeps only the selected columns on show; **View ▸ Reset View** puts the columns, the sort
  and the filter back as they come.
- **Data ▸ Open URL** opens a cell holding a web address in your browser.
- **Data ▸ Compare Cells** opens a tab showing how two selected cells differ, line by line.

## Colours

- **View ▸ Grid ▸ Heatmap** colours the selected number columns by value, pale for the smallest and strong for the largest.
  A column with negative and positive numbers is red below zero and green above; one of only 0 and 1 marks the 1s.
  With everything selected (⌘A), every number column gets one. Choose it again to take it away.
- **View ▸ Grid ▸ Highlight Equal Values** tints every cell holding the focused cell's value.
- What a colour marks is said too: with VoiceOver, a cell says **changed**, **added** or **removed** after its column's
  name, for pending changes and for a comparison's rows, and a compared cell's help gives the other side's value.

## Text, tree and charts

- **View ▸ Grid ▸ View As ▸ Text** shows the rows as text in the copy format (**Edit ▸ Copy As**: TSV at first, or CSV, JSON,
  Markdown, SQL INSERT…), with the column names; **Tree** shows them as JSON, a row per item, with JSON columns opened
  up. **Table** goes back. Both show the first 10,000 rows. In a tree (here or in the value panel), double-click an
  object or array to open or close it; right-click to copy a value or to open or close every one.
- **View ▸ Grid ▸ Chart** draws the rows as a bar, line, area, pie, scatter or histogram chart of a number column, by another
  column. Choose the kind and columns above the chart; point at it to read a value. Bars add up the values of each
  label and show the first 30 labels; a pie shows eight slices and puts the rest in **Other**. Lines, areas and points
  by a date column go in date order along a date axis; by a text column, along the row numbers. A chart covers the
  first 10,000 rows of those loaded, and under it, and in its picture, says so when that leaves rows out. **Save as
  PNG…** saves a picture of it. Pie charts need macOS 14 or later.

## Column Summary

**Data ▸ Column Summary…** (also on a header's right-click menu) counts the focused column's distinct values and NULLs,
finds its smallest and largest values, and lists its 50 most frequent values with how often each appears. For a table
the server works this out over all its rows within the filter; it asks first when the table is larger than 2 GB.
Click a value to show only the rows that hold it (it is added to the filter). For a query result it counts the rows
you have.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/editors.html

# Change tables, views and routines

AirSQL edits a table's structure in a form, and views, procedures, functions, triggers and events as the CREATE
statement that makes them. Nothing changes on the server until you apply, and the SQL that will run is always shown
first.

## The table editor

Open it from a table's **Open Structure**, or make a new table with **Database ▸ Create Table…**. A table editor has seven
parts, chosen at the top:

- **Columns**: name, type (the types your server has), length or ENUM values, unsigned, NULL, default, extra (counts up
  by itself, follows updates, or is generated from an expression), collation and comment. Drag rows to reorder the
  columns.
- **Indexes**: primary key, unique, plain, full-text and spatial indexes. Write their columns separated by commas:
  `email(10)` indexes the first 10 characters, `created_at DESC` sorts down. **Using** chooses BTREE or HASH, and **Visible** off
  keeps an index up to date while queries leave it alone (INVISIBLE on MySQL, IGNORED on MariaDB). In the Columns list, right-click
  selected columns for **New Index from Columns**, **New Unique Index from Columns** and **Add to Index**.
- **Foreign keys**: this table's columns, the table they point at and its columns, and what happens on update and on
  delete.
- **Used by**: the foreign keys of other tables that point at this one, from the databases read so far. Double-click one to open
  that table.
- **Checks**: conditions every row must satisfy. On MariaDB, a check written with a column belongs to that column and
  stays with it when the column changes.
- **Partitions**: the partitions the server has, with their rows and sizes, and the PARTITION BY clause. Edit the clause to add or change
  partitions; empty it to remove them and keep the rows. Changing them copies the table, and rows that fit no partition stop the change.
- **Options**: the table's name, engine, default collation, row format, next AUTO_INCREMENT number and comment.

**+** adds a row, **−** removes the selected rows (or press Delete), and a right-click offers the same. New rows show in
green and changed ones in amber until you apply. **Edit ▸ Undo** takes back a change; **Revert** takes back all of them.
Drag columns to put them in another order, or press ⌃⇧⌘↑ and ⌃⇧⌘↓. ⌘C copies the selected rows as the lines of a CREATE TABLE; ⌘V in this list, here or in another table's editor, adds them
as new rows.

Under the lists, the SQL that Apply would run updates as you type. When something can't work yet (a VARCHAR without a
length, two columns of one name, an emoji in a name, which the server would keep as `?`), it says what to fix instead.

## Apply

**Apply** (⌘S) shows the statements in the [SQL preview](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/sql-preview.html) first; **Open in Query Tab** there puts them in a query tab
instead of running them. Then they run one at a time on a
connection of their own, and the editor reads the table back from the server.

- MySQL and MariaDB can't roll table changes back: each statement takes effect as it runs. When there are several, the
  preview says so; if one fails, the ones before it stay done, and the editor shows what is left to do.
- A changed foreign key is dropped in a statement of its own first: neither server takes a drop and an add of the same
  key in one statement.
- Dropping a column deletes its values, and changing a column's type converts them: the preview warns about both.
- A large table may be copied while it changes, and writes to it wait until that is done.

## Views, procedures, functions, triggers and events

Open one from the tree, or start a new one from **Database ▸ New Object ▸ New Object**. The editor shows its CREATE statement, as the
server keeps it, to edit as text, with its head as fields above it:

- **Procedures and functions**: name, return type, data access, security, deterministic, comment, and the parameters, which **+**, **−**
  and the arrows add, remove and reorder.
- **Triggers**: name, before or after, insert, update or delete, and the table.
- **Events**: name, enabled or disabled, whether it stays after its last run, comment, and the schedule: every so often, with when it
  starts and ends, or once. A bare date and time gets its quotes; anything else is an expression.
- **Views**: name, algorithm, security and check option.

The fields and the code stay in step, and ⌘Z in the code takes a field's change back. The fields rewrite only the head, so the
body stays as you typed it, though a comment between the head's clauses goes. When the head isn't one the form can read (it is still being typed, say),
the fields turn off until it is.

- **Runs as** chooses its DEFINER: the account it was created with, or you. Keeping another account's DEFINER needs the
  SET_USER_ID privilege on MySQL, or SET USER on MariaDB.
- Apply runs it in its database, under the sql_mode it was created with (and an event under its time zone), so it
  behaves as before. The footer shows those settings.
- MariaDB replaces it in one statement (CREATE OR REPLACE). MySQL replaces a view the same way, but drops a procedure,
  function, trigger or event first: if the new code fails, the old one is gone. Your code stays in the editor to fix and
  apply again, and **Revert** puts the old code back.
- **Run…** on a procedure or function opens a CALL or SELECT of it in a query tab, for the code the server has: apply your changes first.
- The code has the tab's editor: line numbers, completion, Comment Lines (⌘/), Format SQL and the matching bracket.
- When the server refuses the code, the place it points to is underlined in red, with the message on hover, until you
  change the text.
- Renaming it in the code makes the new one and then drops the old one.

## The ER diagram

**Database ▸ Diagram ▸ ER Diagram** draws a database's tables with their keys. Tables that point at nothing come first on the left,
and each table sits right of the tables its foreign keys point at; lines go from a key's column to the table it points
at, virtual foreign keys you added in a table's rows included ([Virtual foreign keys](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/table-data.html#foreign-key-labels-and-virtual-foreign-keys)).
Tables with no keys come last.

Click a table to select it (⌘ or ⇧ click adds more; the arrow keys move between tables), double-click it to open it in the
table editor, and right-click it for **Open Structure**, **Open Data**, **Copy Name** and the diagram's own commands (⌘C copies
the selected table's name too), or the empty space to export. Pinch, ⌘+ and ⌘− zoom, ⌘0 goes back to actual size and **Fit** shows
the whole diagram; ⌘F goes to the find field, where typing part of a name selects that table and Return goes to the next. ⌘R
reads the schema again.

### Boxes and saved diagrams

Drag a box to move it, with any others selected; ⌥ and the arrow keys do the same from the keyboard. ⌘Z takes a move back. A
diagram remembers where its boxes are: it is kept on this Mac, never on the server.

A database can have several diagrams, chosen in **Diagram**. The first always shows every table.

- **Diagram of Selected Tables** in a table's right-click menu in the tree makes a diagram of only those tables, and **Diagram
  of Neighbours** adds every table that touches them by a foreign key.
- **Add Table** adds one more, or drag tables onto the diagram from the tree. **Add Neighbours** adds what touches the selected
  boxes (on the whole database's diagram it makes a new diagram of them), and **Remove from Diagram** takes boxes off; the tables
  themselves aren't touched.
- **New Diagram from Selection…** keeps the selected boxes, or all of them, under a name. **Database ▸ Diagram** also has Rename and
  Delete, which asks first: a deleted diagram's layout can't be got back.
- **Arrange** lays the boxes out again, **Left to Right**, **Top to Bottom** or as a **Grid**, and forgets where you moved them.
- **Show** chooses **All Columns**, **Keys Only** or **Names Only**, and turns **Comments** and **Virtual Keys** on or off.

**Export** saves the diagram as a PNG, or as text for other tools: Mermaid, which many docs sites and wikis draw, PlantUML, Graphviz
DOT, GraphML and draw.io (the last two keep where your boxes are). **Print Diagram…** fits it on one page.

## CREATE statements of several objects

**Copy CREATE** works on several selected objects, as one script. **Open CREATE in Query Tab** puts that script in a new query tab;
nothing runs until you run it.

**SQL Generator…**, on a database or on selected objects, shows the statements that recreate them and keeps them up to date as you
change its options: IF NOT EXISTS and OR REPLACE where your server takes them, Skip DEFINER, database names, and whether to keep
indexes, foreign keys, the AUTO_INCREMENT number and the tables' triggers. Tables come first, then views, routines, triggers and events,
with foreign key checks off around several tables so that their order doesn't matter, and DELIMITER lines round routines.

**Copy** and **Open in Query Tab** take the whole script. **Save to Folder…** writes a `.sql` file per object: all in one folder, in a
folder per kind, in folders by database and kind, or numbered in the order they run. Files of the same name are replaced.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/client-tools.html

# Export, restore, copy and import

AirSQL backs up and moves data with your own `mysqldump` and `mysql` (or MariaDB's `mariadb-dump` and `mariadb`)
when you have them, and with its own code when you don't. Every command here is in the **Tools** and **File** menus
and in a connection's right-click menu in the sidebar.

## Which programs AirSQL uses

**Settings ▸ Client Tools** shows the programs AirSQL found and their versions. It looks in Homebrew's folders
(`/opt/homebrew/opt/mysql-client/bin` and the like, on Apple silicon and Intel), `/usr/local/mysql/bin` (MySQL's
installer), MAMP and your `PATH`. Leave the fields empty and AirSQL picks, for each server, the tools of its family
(MariaDB's for MariaDB, MySQL's for MySQL) closest to its version. Choose a program to always use that one.

A `.csv`, `.tsv`, `.xlsx` or `.json` dropped on the window (or a `.csv` or `.xlsx` on the Dock icon) opens Import File with the file chosen, and a `.sql.gz` opens Run SQL
File the same way; nothing runs until you press the sheet's button.

Export, Restore, Run SQL File, Copy to Another Server and Import File each open in a window of their own, which you can
move aside to keep working. Closing it while it runs asks first; disconnecting the connection it uses, or quitting, says
it is running and stops it.

Each window says how well its tool suits the server: **✓ suits the server**, a warning (another family's tool, or an
older version than the server), or why it can't be used (not there, too old: AirSQL needs MySQL 5.7 or MariaDB 10.3
tools or newer). The tool you pick in one is remembered for that connection: it shows, and can be changed, in the
connection editor's Options tab.

No tools at all? Install MySQL's or MariaDB's client tools (for example `brew install mysql-client`), then choose
**Find Again**. Until then, Export and Run SQL File use AirSQL's own code.

## Export a database

**Tools ▸ Export…** (or right-click a connection ▸ Export…).

1. Tick the databases or tables to export. Space ticks the selected rows; right-click for Include All, Include None and
   Include Only These. The filter above the list shows only the tables with that text, each on its own line, so ticks
   reach only what you see; what's ticked stays ticked when you clear it. One database exports without `CREATE DATABASE`, so you can restore it under any name; several
   databases export whole, each with its own name.
2. Choose the content (structure and data, structure only, data only) and the options: one consistent snapshot
   (`--single-transaction`), binary as hex, gzip, `DROP TABLE` before each table, and views, routines, triggers and
   events.
3. Pick the tool (**Choose…** beside it finds a `mysqldump` or `mariadb-dump` anywhere on this Mac, and Restore and Run
   SQL File take a `mysql` or `mariadb` the same way), where to save the file, and any extra options of your own (`--skip-comments`, `--where=…`).
4. The box under the form shows the exact command line of the tool you picked, and **Copy Command** copies it. AirSQL's
   built-in export runs no command, so the box says what it does and the button isn't there.
5. **Output** says where it goes: **One file**, **The clipboard** (small dumps, up to 32 MB) or **A folder, a file per
   object**. In a folder each table, view, routine, trigger and event gets its own `.sql` that restores on its own, read
   in the same snapshot. Choose CSV, TSV, JSON, JSON Lines or Excel in the menu beside it for a data file per ticked
   table instead: column names first, every row, and the SQL options turn off.
6. **Export**. The window shows the table being written, the bytes so far and the time left. **Stop** ends it.

The dump goes into a hidden file next to the one you chose and takes its name only when it is complete, so a stopped
or failed export never leaves half a file. When it is done, **Show in Finder** shows you the file.

**AirSQL (built in)** in the Tool menu writes the SQL itself, through a connection of its own: the tables' `CREATE`
statements, their rows as `INSERT`s (binary as hex), then views, routines, triggers and events, all read in one
consistent snapshot. Its files restore with `mysql` or with Run SQL File.

MySQL's `mysqldump` runs with `--set-gtid-purged=OFF`, so a dump from a server with GTIDs goes back to that server
without failing on `SET GTID_PURGED`. A replica built from such a dump needs its GTID position set by hand: add
`--set-gtid-purged=ON` under the extra options if that's what the dump is for.

### What goes in the SQL

- **Rows as** writes `INSERT`, `INSERT IGNORE`, `REPLACE`, or `DELETE` then `INSERT` for each table, and **at most … KB
  each** caps the size of one statement, for a server with a small `max_allowed_packet`.
- **Add CREATE DATABASE and USE** makes one database restore under its own name; several always do.
- **Add DROP DATABASE first** deletes the whole database of that name when the file is restored. It is off while only
  some tables are ticked, so a file can't take the other tables with it.
- **Remove DEFINER** leaves the account out of views, routines, triggers and events, so a server without that account
  takes them; **Remove AUTO_INCREMENT values** leaves out each table's next value; **A transaction per table** speeds up
  restoring InnoDB tables.

Those last three, `DELETE` before the rows, a folder and the clipboard are AirSQL's own export's: with a dump tool chosen,
the note says so and **Use AirSQL's Built-in** switches.

## Restore a dump, or run a .sql file

**Tools ▸ Restore…** runs a `.sql` or `.sql.gz` file with your `mysql` or `mariadb`; **File ▸ Run SQL File…** opens the
same sheet with AirSQL's own runner, which splits the file into statements as `mysql` does (`DELIMITER` included) and
runs them one at a time. Compressed files are read through `/usr/bin/gzip`.

1. Choose the file and the database it runs in.
2. Choose what happens on an error: stop at the first one (what ran before it stays), or go on and count them
   (`--force`).
3. **Restore** (or **Run**).

Before anything runs, AirSQL reads the whole file for the statements that decide where it writes: `USE`, `CREATE
DATABASE`, `DROP DATABASE`, and `SET GTID_PURGED` (which dumps made in AirSQL leave out). When the file switches to
another database than the one you chose, drops a database, or sets GTID_PURGED, or when the database it writes to has
tables already, the SQL preview sheet says so and asks first (Settings ▸ Safety ▸ *Ask before Restore…*). On a
production connection it always asks.
Progress is the share of the file read, so it is real for compressed files too.

## Copy to another server

**Tools ▸ Copy to Another Server…** copies databases or tables straight from one connection to another, through a
session on each: no file in between.

- **To** and **Database**: the connection and the database the copy goes into (made if it isn't there). One database
  can take another name; views and routines follow the new name.
- **Replace tables that are there** drops the other server's tables of the same name first. It is off unless you tick
  it, and the SQL preview asks before it runs. Copies to a production connection always ask.
- If a statement fails, the copy stops; what was copied before it stays.

## Import a file

**File ▸ Import File…**, or **Import from Clipboard…** for rows copied from a spreadsheet or a text file.

1. Choose the file, or **Paste** the clipboard. CSV and other delimited text, Excel workbooks (`.xlsx`, the first sheet)
   and JSON (an array of objects, or one object a line) all work. AirSQL guesses the separator and shows the first
   rows as they'll be read, at the bottom of the window.
2. Choose the table. Each column takes a field of the file, matched by name when the first row names the columns, by
   position when it doesn't, or **Leave out** to take its default.
   Or choose **New Table…** at the end of the menu: AirSQL reads every value and proposes a `CREATE TABLE` you can edit.
   Only what the server stores unchanged becomes a number or a date: `007`, `+44` and `01/02/2026` stay text. Every
   column allows NULL, and no key is guessed: add one in the box if you want it.
3. **Import**. The rows go in one transaction: if one fails (a duplicate key, a value the column refuses), none of the
   file stays, and the message says which records. A new table stays, empty.

For text files, **Format** chooses the separator (or **Other**, any one character), the quotes and the encoding;
**Automatic** reads UTF-8, UTF-16 with a BOM, and Windows-1252 for what isn't UTF-8. **Skip rows** drops a title above the
table, **Trim spaces** tidies fields without quotes, and **Backslash escapes** reads MySQL's own `\"` inside quotes.

Empty fields and a `NULL` without quotes become NULL unless you untick it (AirSQL's own CSV writes the text NULL in
quotes, so the two come back apart), and a whole `0x…` field in a BLOB or BINARY column becomes its bytes. **Numbers use a
decimal comma** reads `1.234,56` as `1234.56` in number columns. In JSON, `null` is always NULL, `true` and `false` are 1
and 0, and nested values go in as their JSON.

**Rows** says what happens when things go wrong:

- **Stop at a duplicate** undoes the import; **Skip duplicates** keeps the row already there (`INSERT IGNORE`, which also
  lets the server adjust values that don't fit, so check its warnings); **Replace duplicates** puts the file's row in its
  place (`REPLACE`).
- **Delete the table's rows first** deletes them in the same transaction, after a warning, so a failed import brings them
  back. On MyISAM and other tables without transactions it can't: the preview warns of that, and a failed import says what stays.
- **Skip rows the server refuses** keeps the good rows and writes the others, each with the reason, to a CSV in
  Downloads; **Show Skipped Rows** finds it. A lost connection or a deadlock still stops the import and undoes it.

### Copy a result into a table

Right-click a result ▸ **Copy Result to Table…** (or **Query ▸ Result ▸ Copy Result to Table…**) opens the same window with the
selected rows, or all of them, into a table of this connection or a new one. NULLs, empty text and bytes stay apart.

AirSQL sends the rows as `INSERT`s: `LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE` stays off.

## Flush

**Tools ▸ Flush** clears the server's host cache, closes and reopens its logs, reloads the grant tables, closes its open
tables or resets its status counters, each after the SQL preview. They need the `RELOAD` privilege and are off on a
read-only connection.

**Lock All Tables for Reading…** stops every write on the server (`FLUSH TABLES WITH READ LOCK`), for a consistent copy of
its files. AirSQL keeps the lock on a connection of its own while a sheet says so; **Unlock** releases it, and so does
quitting. Should its session end first, Unlock says so: don't count on a copy made under that lock. It is off for agents.

## Open the mysql command line in Terminal

**Tools ▸ Open in Terminal** opens Terminal running `mysql` (or `mariadb`) on the connection, in its database. On a
[read-only connection](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/connections.html#add-or-edit-a-connection) it starts with `SET SESSION TRANSACTION READ ONLY`, as
AirSQL's own sessions do, so a slip can't change anything there. Exports get it too, where the dump tool knows how
(MySQL 8.4's and later); restores, Run SQL File, imports and copies into a read-only connection are refused.

## Your password stays private

The client tools get the login from a temporary option file that only you can read (file mode 0600, in a private
folder in AirSQL's Application Support folder), passed as `--defaults-file`, so `~/.my.cnf` and `/etc/my.cnf` don't
change where they connect. The password is never on the command line, in the environment, or in the command shown.
AirSQL removes the file as soon as the tool has read it: once a dump has started writing, once a restore is reading
its input, ten seconds after Terminal starts `mysql`; and anything left behind at the next launch.

Over TCP the tools check TLS the way the connection asks: MySQL's with `--ssl-mode`, MariaDB's with `--ssl` and
`--ssl-verify-server-cert`. A tool never runs without its certificate check. A certificate you trusted (pinned) is
checked by MariaDB tools that take `--ssl-fp`, which get its fingerprint; AirSQL asks the tool's `--help` whether it
does. Other tools run on such a connection only if it has a CA file and checks the authority, against that file.
MySQL's tools check certificates only against a CA file. When the tool can't check the server, the window says what
to do and **Use AirSQL's Built-in** switches to AirSQL's own export or runner, which check it as AirSQL does; such a
tool is never picked for you.

With a certificate you trusted and no CA file, Export, Restore and Run SQL File also offer MySQL's tools an unticked
box, **Run without checking the certificate**. The connection is encrypted but can't prove it's this server, so the
login and the dump could be exposed, and a restore's data goes to a server that isn't proved. The tool then runs with
`--ssl-mode=REQUIRED`, never without TLS; the tick lasts one run, is never saved, clears when you change the tool, and
the run is noted in the SQL log. MariaDB's older tools don't get the box, as without a check they can't insist on TLS.
Open in Terminal follows the same rules with an alert each time instead of a box: **Cancel** is the default, and **Open
Without Checking** goes on with TLS required, saving nothing. Copy to Another Server needs neither: it uses no client
tool, and AirSQL's own sessions check the certificate on both sides.

Client tools reach SSH and proxy routes through the connection's private socket once AirSQL is connected through them.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/compare.html

# Compare

**Tools ▸ Compare…** opens a window that compares two servers, two databases, or two tables or other objects, on the
same server or on two different connections, such as production against staging or MySQL 8 against MariaDB. A
connection that isn't connected connects when you choose it, asking for a password or to trust a certificate on the
compare window as the main window would; each side then works through its own route, on a session of its own. The
compare only reads; nothing changes until you run the sync script yourself.

## Start from the tree

- **Compare With…** in the menu of a connection, database, table, view, routine, trigger or event starts from that row:
  it is the source, and you choose the target.
- **Compare**, with two rows selected (⌘-click), compares them; the first is the source. They can be on two connections.
  Two tables or other objects of one kind compare at once. Two databases or two connections fill the window in and wait
  for you to press Compare, because they can read a lot: you may want to choose what to compare first.

Both are in the **Tools** menu too.

## Run a compare

1. Choose the **level** at the left: **Servers**, **Databases**, or **Objects** (two tables, or two other objects).
2. Choose the **source** on the left and the **target** on the right: a connection, then one of its databases (or
   type its name), then at the third level an object from the list. The sync script makes the target like the source;
   **Swap** turns them around.
3. Choose what to compare: **Structure and Data**, **Structure** or **Data**.
4. Click **Compare** (⌘R). The bar under the setup shows the table and chunk being checked, and **Cancel** (⌘.)
   stops the compare; the statement running on each server is stopped too. The work is also listed in the main
   window's activity list.

The summary says how many tables match, differ in structure, or are only on one side, how many rows differ, and how
much of the data had to come over the network. The list shows what differs first: **only source** and **only target**
for objects on one side, **structure**, **data**, then **match**. The filter above it narrows it by name, and **Hide
Matching** leaves only what differs. Click an object to see it; double-click it, or press Return, to see its rows when
they differ.

The two definitions scroll together. Changed lines stand against each other, with the words that changed marked. **↑**
and **↓** (⇧F7 and F7) go to the previous and next difference. **Unified** shows one text instead: the target's lines the
script takes out (`-`), the source's it puts in (`+`). With the **Whitespace in Definitions** rule on, lines that differ
only in spacing aren't marked.

## Two servers

At the **Servers** level, each side is a connection. Every database is paired by name (without case, where either
server ignores it), leaving out `information_schema`, `performance_schema`, `mysql` and `sys`, and each pair is compared
in turn with the same settings. The summary counts the pairs that match, differ and are on one side, and the rows and
objects that differ across them. A pair that can't be read says why, and the others go on.

Double-click a pair, or press Return, to open it: it shows as a compare of those two databases, with its list, its
details and its sync script. **All Databases** above the list returns to the pairs, counting what you did there. A script
belongs to one pair, so **Sync Script…** needs a pair open. **Export Report…** at this level covers every pair.

## Two tables or objects

At the **Objects** level, each side is one object, by any name: `orders` against `orders_old`, in one
database or in two. Both must be of one kind.

- **Tables** compare in structure and rows, as in a database compare. **Tables…** chooses the columns to leave out and a
  WHERE. Two tables of one database can't share a foreign key's name, so foreign keys pair up by what they do.
- **Views, routines, triggers, events and sequences** compare by definition, side by side, their own names aside.

The sync script changes only the target, under the target's name: the source's definition is written for it.

## What is compared

- **Structure:** tables (columns, indexes, foreign keys, checks, engine, comment), views, procedures, functions,
  triggers, events and sequences. The **Structure** tab shows both definitions side by side, the lines only one
  side has marked.
- **Data:** the rows of every table both sides have, matched on the primary key, or on a unique key whose columns
  are all NOT NULL. The **Data** tab shows the rows that differ in the [data grid](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/data-grid.html), as a sync would
  change the target: rows only in the source in green (the script inserts them), rows only in the target in red and
  struck through (it deletes them), then rows in both whose differing cells are amber (it updates them); hold the
  pointer over an amber cell to see both values. The line above the rows counts each kind. The grid works as
  elsewhere: select cells or rows with ⌘ and ⇧, copy them in any format (⌘C, **Copy with Headers**, **Copy As**),
  sort by a header, see a long value in the value panel, or save the rows with **Export Rows…**. Tables without such a
  key are still checked as a whole, but their rows can't be matched or synced. Generated columns are left out: their
  values follow from the others.

MySQL and MariaDB write the same thing differently, and the compare reads them alike: `int(11)` and `int`, MariaDB's
JSON (a LONGTEXT with a check) and MySQL's, `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` and `current_timestamp()`, `NO ACTION` and
`RESTRICT`, check constraints the two servers name differently. Each flavour writes a view's or routine's body its own
way, though (MariaDB adds `COLLATE` to a function's `RETURNS`), so the same one on MySQL and on MariaDB can still show as
different.

### Ignore rules

**Ignore Rules** chooses differences the compare doesn't count. The first four are on at first:

- **AUTO_INCREMENT Values**: tables' next AUTO_INCREMENT values.
- **DEFINER**: who views, routines, triggers and events run as. The script then leaves DEFINER out, so they run as
  whoever runs the script.
- **Collations and Character Sets** of tables and columns (MySQL 8 and MariaDB have different defaults).
- **Whitespace in Definitions**: spaces and line breaks in bodies, outside quoted text.
- **Column Order**: the order of a table's columns.
- **Letter Case in Definitions**: upper and lower case in bodies, outside quoted text.
- **Definitions**: what views, routines, triggers and events say. Only whether each exists counts.

### Tables…

**Tables…** lists the source's tables, once a source and database are chosen, so a long first compare can be limited.
Untick a table to leave it out, give the target table it should be compared with when it was renamed there, list
columns whose values shouldn't count (such as `updated_at`), or add a WHERE condition for its rows on both sides. Type
in the filter to find a table; **Compare All** and **Compare None** tick and untick the tables shown. Double-click a
table to tick or untick it, or right-click the selected tables (⌘ and ⇧ select several) for Compare and Leave Out. **Leave Out of Next Compare** in an object's menu unticks it
too.

## How the data compare stays fast

Each server sums up the rows of a chunk of the table (10,000 rows by key order) as a row count and a total of 64-bit
row hashes, computed from SHA-256. Only a chunk whose sums differ is looked at more closely: it is split into smaller
chunks, and for the small ones that still differ each row's key and hash come over, then only the rows that differ.
A million identical rows are checked without fetching any.

The hashes tell apart values that careless checksums mix up: a NULL and an empty string, values moved from one column
to another, `'a'` and `'A'` or `'a '` under a case-insensitive collation, the same text in latin1 and utf8mb4 (which
counts as the same). Both sessions use time zone `+00:00`, so TIMESTAMP values compare by the moment they stand for.
Floats, decimals written with another scale and JSON with other spacing or key order are compared as values.

## The sync script

Each object that differs has a tick in the list. Untick it, or use **Include in Sync Script** in its menu, and the script,
**Copy Sync Script** and the changeset leave it out; what it depends on is up to you.

The **Sync script** box shows the statements for the selected object; **Copy Sync Script** copies them. **Sync
Script…** opens the whole script in a [console](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/console.html) tab of the target named “Sync script”, to read (it can't
be edited there; **Save As…** keeps a copy). It never runs on its own: **Run** in that tab brings the compare window
back with the script in the [SQL preview](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/sql-preview.html), where you can copy it, run it on the target, or cancel. It
runs:

1. `USE` the target database and `SET time_zone = '+00:00'`;
2. the structure changes, in order: foreign keys and objects that go or change are dropped first, then new tables,
   `ALTER TABLE`, views (after the views they use), foreign keys, routines, triggers and events. MySQL and MariaDB
   commit each structure change on its own: they can't be rolled back;
3. the row changes in one transaction: DELETE (children before parents), then UPDATE and INSERT (parents first). Each
   statement must change exactly the rows it names; if one doesn't, because the target changed since the compare,
   everything in the transaction is rolled back. Tables on MyISAM, Aria or MEMORY can't roll back, and the preview
   warns about them.

**Destructive steps are left out** unless you tick **Include destructive steps**: dropping tables, columns, indexes,
checks, foreign keys and other objects only the target has, deleting rows only the target has, and column changes
that could cut or refuse values (a shorter type, NOT NULL). Each destructive statement is marked with a
`-- Destructive:` comment, and the preview's button turns red.

Rows of tables only in the source come with their `CREATE TABLE`. New columns of existing tables get their default
values: after running the script, compare again to copy their values. After a sync, AirSQL offers to compare again.

**Save as Changeset…** saves the script as [Liquibase](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/liquibase.html) changesets in a changelog you choose; so does
**Query ▸ Save as Changeset…** in the “Sync script” tab.

## Compare two results, or a result with a table

In a [console](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/console.html), **Compare With…** (a result tab's right-click menu, or **Query ▸ Result ▸ Compare Result With…**) compares
the result shown with another one, row by row:

- **Compare with** offers the other result tabs of the window, this tab's nearest first (a result from another
  query tab, such as the same query on another server, carries that tab's name), then the tables and views of the tab's database.
- **Match rows on** says which columns tell rows apart: the result's key when it has one, a single column, or every
  column (rows then differ only as being on one side). Rows with the same values there are the same row; when several
  share them, they pair up in the order they come.
- The rows that differ open in a result tab of their own, named after the other side (“vs Yesterday”), next to the
  result: rows only in this result green, rows only in the other red and struck through, and in rows on both sides the
  cells that differ amber (hold the pointer over one to see both values). The results bar says how many rows are the
  same. When nothing differs, AirSQL says so instead.

Only the columns both sides have, by name, are compared, with the rules of the data compare: numbers, decimals of
another scale and floats as numbers, JSON as values (MySQL writes it its own way), NULL apart from an empty string. A
table is read up to 100,000 rows; for a larger one, compare the result of a query with a WHERE, or whole tables with
**Tools ▸ Compare…**. Comparing only reads.

## Export the report

**Export Report…** saves what the compare found as **HTML** (to read or send), **CSV** (every difference on its own
line, for a spreadsheet) or **Markdown** (for a ticket). HTML and Markdown list up to 1,000 rows per table.

## Limits

- More than 100,000 differing rows in one table are reported as too many to list, without sync statements for that
  table: narrow the compare with a WHERE, or copy the table instead.
- A server compare keeps every pair's differing rows in memory: on servers that differ a lot, compare **Structure** first.
- A tick is for a whole object: the changes within a table go or stay together.
- Column order and row formats are compared and synced. Partitioning is only noticed on one side: a table partitioned
  differently on both reads the same, and no statement adds or removes it. System versioning isn't compared.
- The data compare reads each side as it goes, not one snapshot: on a busy table it can show rows that changed meanwhile.
- A FLOAT compares by the text the server gives, about six digits: 1.0000001 and 1.0000002 both read `1`.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/agents.html

# AI agents

Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Claude Desktop and other MCP clients can use AirSQL to read your schemas, run read-only
queries, profile tables and propose SQL for you to run. They work through AirSQL on your Mac, so they see only what you
allow, never your passwords, and can't change data.

## Turn agents on

1. Choose **AirSQL ▸ Settings…** (⌘,), then **Agents**, and tick **Allow AI agents to use AirSQL**.
2. Under **Connections**, choose what agents may do with each connection. Every connection starts at **Off**.
3. Add AirSQL to your agent:
   - **Add to Claude Code…** or **Add to Gemini CLI…**: AirSQL shows the exact change to that program's settings
     (`~/.claude.json` or `~/.gemini/settings.json`), and makes it only when you click **Add**, keeping the old file as
     `.airsql-backup`. Restart the program afterwards.
   - Claude Code's plugin: `claude plugin marketplace add kleash/airsql`, then `claude plugin install airsql@airsql`.
   - Claude Desktop: open `airsql.mcpb` from AirSQL's release.
   - Another client: **Copy** gives the command, `/Applications/AirSQL.app/Contents/MacOS/AirSQL --mcp`.

The connection must be connected in AirSQL for an agent to read it.

## Access levels

| Level | Agents may |
|---|---|
| Off | not see the connection at all |
| Schema | read databases, tables, columns, keys and indexes, and find columns by name; put SQL into a query tab |
| Schema + read | also run read-only queries and see query plans, within the row cap and time limit of Settings ▸ Safety |
| Schema + read + analytics | also profile tables, get ten times the rows and four times the time, and save results to files |

**Sample rows** (a separate switch) lets agents see a few rows of each table they describe. Only you can change these:
no agent can, whatever it asks.

## What keeps your data safe

- An agent's statement runs only if AirSQL can prove it reads and nothing more: one SELECT, SHOW, DESCRIBE or
  EXPLAIN, without locking clauses, `INTO`, hints or functions such as `SLEEP` ([what passes](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/read-only-queries.html)).
- It then runs on a session of its own that the server keeps read-only, inside a read-only transaction that is rolled
  back, with a time limit. Even a statement that slipped past the check can't write.
- To change something, an agent puts the SQL into a query tab. Nothing runs until you press Run.
- For more safety still, connect with a database user that can only read.

## MongoDB connections

On a MongoDB connection with **Schema + read** (or analytics), agents get tools of their own: find, aggregate, count,
distinct, the lists of databases, collections and indexes, sizes, and a summary of a sample of documents. They can't
write: every request is checked before it is sent, and refused if it would run JavaScript (`$where`, `$function`) or
write (`$out`, `$merge`), uses a pipeline stage AirSQL hasn't vetted, or reaches MongoDB's own databases (admin,
local, config) or `system` collections. Each runs with the time limit and document cap of Settings ▸ Safety, and on a
replica set inside a transaction that is always cancelled, so even a write that got past the check is refused by the
server. For more safety still, connect with a user that has only the `read` role. Documents, distinct values and sizes
reach the agent as Extended JSON text, so a field's order and a number's type (`2.0` stays a double) are kept.

With **Schema** access an agent can ask for a whole database in one summary: each collection's count, size, indexes
and validator, its fields with their types (and with Schema + read their common values and ranges), views, and the
references between collections (orders' `customerId` to `customers._id`), each checked by looking up a few sampled
values. It can ask how MongoDB would run a query without running it (explain's plan), or run it for its figures.
When a query names a field not in the collection's sample, or compares a date with a string, the reply warns and
names the nearest field; a server's error says which stage and which word it didn't know. With **Schema + read +
analytics**, finds and pipelines can go to a file in the agent export folder (Settings ▸ Agents), never elsewhere.

To propose a query or a change, an agent opens a new collection tab with the query bar filled in, or a pipeline tab,
titled "… · proposed by" the agent and with a note that says so (**Dismiss** hides it). Nothing runs, and nothing is
read, until you press Run; a pipeline that writes (`$merge`, `$out`) still shows you its preview first, and is refused
on a read-only connection. The agent can read what a MongoDB tab holds and how its last run went; the documents
loaded in it only when the connection allows Schema + read.

## Agents in AirSQL's windows

Agents can also work in AirSQL's windows as you do: open tabs, choose menu commands, fill in sheets, take screenshots.
Whatever that would change waits for you:

- Anything that would run on a server (Run in a query tab, Apply, a compare's sync, Restore, Copy, Import, Commit)
  first shows the SQL preview sheet, marked **Asked by** and the agent's name. Only you can press its Run; the agent
  can only decline. Statements that AirSQL proves only read run without asking.
- Agents can't change Settings, shortcuts, agent access, a connection's colour, read-only switch, server, route, login, TLS,
  startup SQL or safety settings, nor save files, start an export, save a password, trust a certificate, paste from
  your clipboard, quit AirSQL or press a button marked destructive (Don't Save, Disconnect with a transaction open).
  Text an agent types into a query tab of a Production connection is shown to you first.
- On connections whose agent access doesn't include reading, grids and results, the filters their values go into,
  the tab's messages (a server's error can quote a value), query plans, server accounts and the SQL preview's statements are
  hidden from the agent's snapshots and screenshots; the SQL log's text and Query History's **All connections** always are. A cell's right-click menu never shows an agent the
  cell's value or your clipboard's text.

**Settings ▸ Safety ▸ Ask before agents change anything** (on by default, per connection in its Safety tab) turns the
asking off; what is yours alone stays yours.

## Ask your agent from the editor

**Query ▸ Ask an Agent** copies a request to paste into your agent: **Explain This**, **Fix the Last Error**, **Make This
Faster** or **Write SQL…**. AirSQL has no AI of its own, and nothing leaves your Mac from here.

The request names the tab and the selected lines and holds no SQL. The agent reads the tab with its usual tool, at the
access the connection allows and with passwords masked, and proposes SQL in a new tab for you to run. A request can't give
an agent any more than that. The items are off while agents are off or can't see the connection.

## See what agents did

The agents' item in the status bar says what they're doing. Click it (or choose **Tools ▸ Agents ▸ Agent Activity**)
for every call since AirSQL opened, with how it ended. A call that reads a database also shows in Activity, where
**Cancel** stops it. **Turn Agents Off** in that popover (or in Tools ▸ Agents) stops them at once.

**View ▸ Agent Results** opens the connection's Agent tab: every statement agents ran on it with `run_queries`, newest
last, and under the list the rows the selected one got, read-only and no more than the agent got. Double-click a
`run_queries` call in Agent Activity to open the tab at its statements. Double-click a statement (or choose **Query ▸
Open in New Query**) to put it in a new query tab, where you can change it and run it yourself. The tab keeps the
last 100 statements since AirSQL opened.

## Files agents save

With analytics, agents can save query results as CSV or JSON files. They go only to the **Agent Exports** folder in
AirSQL's settings folder (Settings ▸ Agents ▸ Exports ▸ Show in Finder), readable by you alone.

## The fine print

Agents reach AirSQL through a socket in AirSQL's settings folder that only you can open, with a key that changes each
time AirSQL starts. Other programs running as you could read that key too, as with any app of yours.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/liquibase.html

# Liquibase changelogs

AirSQL writes [Liquibase](https://www.liquibase.com) changelogs in Liquibase's **formatted SQL**: plain SQL with
`--changeset author:id` lines, which Liquibase reads as it is. You can write one of a whole database, save a compare's
sync script as changesets, or save any change AirSQL shows you before it runs. AirSQL only writes the files: run them
with your own `liquibase` (`liquibase update`, `liquibase rollback-count 1`…).

## A changelog of a database

**Tools ▸ Generate Liquibase Changelog…** writes a changelog of a database of the connection the window is about.

- **Content**: **Structure** writes the objects' DDL, **Rows** their rows as DML, **Both** the two.
- The list holds the database's tables, views, procedures, functions, triggers, events and sequences, each ticked.
  Untick what you don't want; space ticks the selected rows, double-click ticks one, and the right-click menu
  includes all, none or the selected rows; the filter above the list narrows it, and all and none then mean the
  objects shown. For **DML**, tick **Rows** for the tables whose rows to write, and type a
  **WHERE** condition (double-click the cell) to write only some of them, such as `active = 1`.
- **Author** and **Ids** make each `--changeset` line (see [Settings](#settings) below). **Rollback** adds the
  `--rollback` line that undoes each object. **Skip what already exists** adds preconditions that mark a changeset
  as ran, rather than run it, when its object is already in the database: handy for a database made before you used
  Liquibase.
- **Files**: one file, or a folder with a file per changeset and `db.changelog-master.yaml`, which includes them in
  order: point Liquibase at that one.

The preview beside the form shows the changelog as it will be written. **Save Changelog** reads each table's rows
then, in key order, from one consistent snapshot; the work is listed in the activity list, with **Stop**. Nothing is
left behind if it fails or you stop it.

### What the changelog holds, in order

Each object gets one changeset, in an order that runs cleanly on an empty database:

1. sequences, then tables, each without its foreign keys and without its next AUTO_INCREMENT value;
2. the tables' rows (parents before children), as INSERTs of 100 rows each;
3. the foreign keys, one changeset each (`ALTER TABLE … ADD CONSTRAINT`);
4. functions and procedures, then views (each after the views it reads), triggers and events.

Rows come before foreign keys and triggers, so neither gets in their way. A changeset of rows first sets the session
as the rows were read: in UTC (TIMESTAMP values stay as they were), without strict mode (zero dates load) and with
`NO_AUTO_VALUE_ON_ZERO` (a 0 in an AUTO_INCREMENT column stays 0); it puts the session's own settings back at its end.
A table with zero dates or TIMESTAMP defaults gets the same around its `CREATE TABLE`.

Attributes are added only where they are needed:

- A procedure, function, trigger or event holds semicolons of its own, so its changeset says `splitStatements:false`
  and runs it as one statement (or ends it with `//` and says `endDelimiter://`, as you choose in Settings).
- `stripComments:false` keeps comments Liquibase would otherwise remove, such as MySQL's `/*!80023 INVISIBLE */`.
- Views are written as `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW` with `runOnChange:true`: edit a view in the changelog and Liquibase
  replaces it.
- A comment line in a routine that Liquibase would read as one of its own (`-- rollback …`, `-- changeset …`)
  becomes a `#` comment, which MySQL and MariaDB read the same way.

Every changeset AirSQL writes is read back the way Liquibase reads it before it is saved; if Liquibase would split it
differently from how it runs here, AirSQL says so and doesn't write it.

## Save a change as a changeset

When the [SQL preview](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/sql-preview.html) shows a change (the table editor, a view or routine, a sync script), tick
**Save as Liquibase changeset**: once the change has run, a sheet shows the changeset. In the query tab, select the
statements (or put the insertion point in one) and choose **Query ▸ Save as Changeset…**. In the compare window,
**Save as Changeset…** (or **Query ▸ Save as Changeset…** in its “Sync script” tab) saves the sync script: a changeset
per structure step and one per run of row changes on a table, destructive steps saying so in their `--comment`.
